#4715. How to Survive the Year’s Final Six Weeks

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

It’s that time of year. Whether you like it or not, the holidays are coming up. Turkey Day, Hanukkah, Christmas, and Kwanzaa— the end of the year can mean at least one family gathering. And while such get-togethers can be fun, they can also be stressful and anxiety-producing. Here are four self-care reminders to help you survive the final six weeks of the year.

Reaching for a hug is a common greeting in many family households, but fist bumps are entirely appropriate. They are less invasive and more hygienic. And for children and teens: hugs are not required. For people with histories of unwanted touch, this can be a valuable reminder. Of course, if you are a hugger, then feel free to hug as long as your hugging partner agrees by stretching their arms.

Holiday gatherings can be very stressful events. You can always take a break. Mediate. Go outside. Take a nap. Read a book. Enjoy a family photo album. We often feel we have to absorb every second with our loved ones during a holiday celebration. This is especially true if we don’t see one another often and family members have traveled distances. However, we are at our best when we are not overwhelmed. If you start to feel overextended, take a deep breath and restore yourself. You might even practice a simple meditation to check in with yourself and make sure you are enjoying the experience. If you are not, get curious, ask yourself why, and rejoin the group when your heart feels more open.

Holidays can stir your emotions. They often remind us of loved ones who have passed, treasured childhood memories, and more. You may wonder why you are suddenly feeling a wave of sadness or guilt at a seemingly joyful, celebratory event. It's okay to get emotional. Our brains link holidays to a myriad of emotional states that we may not always feel prepared for or even understand. If you start feeling emotional, remind yourself that it is perfectly normal and that others in the room are also likely feeling emotional, too. If this happens, consider sharing your feelings with a loved one whom you feel safe around.

Participating in a structured activity can also help decrease stress. You can play a game, pull out a deck of cards, or even piece together a puzzle. If you prefer something more active, go outside and toss a ball around. When we focus on a fun activity together, we can often alleviate stress with light-heartedness. If games aren't your thing, being creative might be. Try a craft together, a coloring book, or bake a cake. Connect with loved ones through play.

Gatherings can feel like an obligation, but they are really a gift we give one another. When we take time to see each other in person, share a meal, engage in a holiday tradition, exchange gifts, and check in with one another, we are opening ourselves up to connection. We are choosing to bond. But that decision isn’t a requirement, and if you find yourself feeling that it is, these self-care practices can help you get through the anxiety or discomfort.

#4714. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4712. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4711. The Good News About the Midterm Election

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Democrats are understandably celebrating the “blue wave” that overtook the U.S. in the midterm election, and many Republicans are stunned and disappointed by the magnitude of their losses. Neither response is surprising, of course. However, as a political psychologist, I can’t help but feel that the results should give hope to all Americans, regardless of political leaning. Let me explain why.

For the past couple of decades, pundits have lamented the polarization of American politics. The conventional wisdom has been that we now live in two Americas, one red and one blue, and that never the twain shall meet. Stereotypes of affluent, educated, urban, wine-drinking liberals and working-class, rural, less-educated, beer-drinking, gun-toting conservatives proliferated. Politics seemed to have become a major dividing line between us.

Some political scientists maintained that most Americans are pragmatic moderates and that the level of polarization had been exaggerated, but most media coverage seemed to ignore that point of view. A more nuanced approach suggested that although issue polarization (differences in policy positions) was less pronounced, affective polarization (feelings toward those in the other party) was indeed extreme. In fact, one study documented that hostility toward those in the other political wing was so great that individuals would be more upset about their offspring marrying someone of the other party than marrying someone of a different race. Given the magnitude of the racial divide in the U.S., that was a remarkable finding.

This take on America as a deeply polarized society has some scary implications for our democracy. Democratic nations function successfully when the voters can be counted on to evaluate politicians and their policies. If polarization is so high that voters always approve of the politicians in their own party and disapprove of the ones in the other party, regardless of their actions, then we have a situation in which our government has no accountability. This would mean that politicians would have guaranteed support from their base no matter what. Why even have elections if they end up simply reflecting a count of the number of people in each party? A government of the people and for the people requires that the people pay attention and fairly evaluate whether our leaders are leading us in the right direction.

The recent election indicated that many people who had been supportive of President Trump and his party changed their minds. Their concerns about issues like affordability, an unpopular war in Iran, an extreme crackdown on immigrants suspected of being undocumented, financial support for what many experts consider a genocide in Gaza, to name a few, ended up outweighing their desire to stick with the party they had put in power. Painful as this might seem to Republicans, I would argue that it is better for the country as a whole to have an electorate that does not reflexively vote the same way in every election if there are significant reasons to endorse a change. We have to be able to count on the voters to hold our government accountable.

In American culture, to hold someone accountable is to view them as responsible or to blame for a problem. Extensive research has shown that blame plays a major role in politics. Politicians who are blamed, particularly for the state of the economy and war, tend to pay a price in elections. One of the keys to Trump’s success has been an ability to avoid blame for his actions. Recall his statement during a 2016 campaign rally that he could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot someone and wouldn’t lose any voters. Whether one supports Trump or not, it would be hard to argue that allowing a politician to get away with anything is a good practice. Again, accountability is key to democracy.

Therefore, it would seem to be a positive sign that voters, many of whom hold the president responsible for the problems our country faces, are holding him to account. It means that they are actually thinking about the administration’s policies and evaluating them. Wouldn’t we rather have an electorate that bases its voting on such evaluations instead of reflexively voting for the same person they voted for last time, regardless of the state of the country?

Given the general assumption that the U.S. is involved in a war between red and blue value systems, it is perhaps not surprising that a number of Republican candidates focused on hot-button culture war issues like gender roles, LGBTQ+ rights, and DEI efforts in their campaigns. The goal was to convince Americans that some Democrats do not share mainstream American values. For example, James Talarico was attacked as a “woke” vegan who believes in multiple genders. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed was labeled a jihadist who supported the 9/11 attacks. Such rhetoric is aimed at labeling some candidates as “them” rather than “us” and thereby alienating American voters. Interestingly, that approach does not seem to have succeeded, and it may even have backfired. Though there are a number of possible explanations for this trend, a major factor was likely that American voters are much more focused on the economy and therefore do not pay much attention to such attacks. A more optimistic view is that stereotypes and prejudice do not carry the same power they once did. It is also possible that citizens are simply tired of these types of personal attacks. All three of these possibilities speak well of American voters.

In spite of increased political polarization in the U.S., polls indicate that Americans believe there is more that unites than divides us. It thus stands to reason that we would value an emphasis on unity and civility over division and ugliness. Although the verdict is still out on the degree to which disgust with the nastiness of politics had a role in this election, some pundits have suggested that it was a factor. Most people would likely prefer that politicians focus on the real problems we face as a society rather than tearing each other down.

Particularly notable in this regard was Vivek Ramaswamy’s cruel ad attacking the honesty of Dr. Amy Acton. Although some politicians might relish opportunities to verbally attack their opponents in hopes of instilling fear or revulsion in voters, it appears that many Americans are not buying what they are selling. Ramaswamy’s attack resulted in an outpouring of support for Dr. Acton, and she won the election. An attempt to elicit distrust of Dr. Acton actually gave rise to empathy for her.

Shouldn’t we all prefer civility over nastiness and cruelty, regardless of our political leaning? A number of Republicans were among the critics of Ramaswamy’s ad, suggesting that they are capable of holding fellow partisans accountable and that they would prefer more civil politics.

Overall, we can be more optimistic that our democracy, which has become increasingly threatened by intense hostility across party lines, extreme within-party loyalty, a refusal to hold politicians accountable, divisive culture wars, racial and religious prejudice, and a shocking level of incivility, might be moving in a healthy direction. Hopefully, this trend will continue, and our society can live up to its promise.

#4708. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4707. Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

#4706. The Unexpected Legacy of Childhood Adversity

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Recently I attended the 35th anniversary celebrations of Smile as a Gift—Úsmev ako dar—a charitable organization in Bratislava, Slovakia, that assists children in foster care and children’s homes, as well as families threatened by poverty, violence, imprisonment, or illness.

Slovakia also has a Commissioner for Children, Jozef Miklosko, who is committed to defending children’s rights under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Jozef and I spent many hours talking about Slovak “social orphans," children who have been separated from their parents because of a complicated mixture of neglect, poverty, illness, imprisonment, abuse, family breakdown, and, more recently, displacement by the war in Ukraine. They are now under the care of the social welfare system. Each child has a different history and reacts differently to harsh conditions. But they are all affected. What is happening in Slovakia is happening everywhere. Hundreds of millions of children in every country are vulnerable to adversity. Growing up under such stressful conditions undermines health, development, and learning.

It was only 28 years ago that researchers introduced the concept of adverse childhood experiences, ACEs, as a way of measuring the cumulative effects of childhood adversity. Since then, many studies have shown that ACEs appear to extend across the lifespan, increasing the likelihood of unhealthy behaviors, mental illness, and a range of chronic physical diseases.

Professor Karen Hughes of Bangor University in the UK and her colleagues conducted a particularly thorough review. The 37 studies involved more than a quarter of a million people. They found that more childhood hardship increases the risk of widespread challenges later in life. The links were relatively weak for obesity, physical inactivity, and diabetes; stronger for smoking, heavy drinking, cancer, heart disease, and respiratory illness; and stronger still for mental health problems and risky sexual behavior. But the most disturbing associations were with drug misuse, violence toward others, and violence directed against oneself.

Most Abused Children Abuse Others in Adulthood

Surprisingly, the commonly held belief that children who suffer physical abuse are at increased risk of becoming abusive parents themselves, and that children who have been sexually abused become adult sexual offenders is refuted by many academic studies. Most abused children do not grow up to abuse others.

Scientific research focused for a long time on the risks associated with adversity. The prevailing deficit model described children from high-stress backgrounds as being at risk for impairments in learning and behavior. The intervention goal was to prevent, reduce, or repair the damage.

Recent studies show that damage and adaptation can occur simultaneously. How do some individuals manage to flourish despite painful experiences that leave others struggling? The following brief biographies may throw some light on the subject that academic studies fail to do.

We are all familiar with Charles Dickens, but most of us don’t know that his father was imprisoned for debt, and at 12, Dickens was sent to work in a shoe-blacking factory. The humiliation and insecurity of that experience haunted him and informed much of his writing. He made the suffering of impoverished children one of the great moral themes of his writing.

Abraham Lincoln’s childhood was marked by poverty, exhausting physical labour, and limited schooling. When Lincoln was 9, his mother died. His father remarried a widow with three children. Lucky for young Abe, his stepmother was not the folkloric evil stepmother but a significant positive influence. She encouraged his love of books, treated him affectionately; they shared a close relationship for the rest of her life.

Although their childhoods differed considerably, Charles Dickens, Abraham Lincoln, and many others I don’t have space to mention spent their childhoods in environments that offered limited educational opportunities. However, they shared an awareness of the limitations of their present lives and found people who encouraged them and helped them to progress. Their childhood experiences shaped what they noticed, cared about, and fought for.

In some instances, having been powerless may make a person particularly aware of the powerlessness of others. Unfair treatment may motivate some individuals to commit to fair play and justice.

While we cannot deny that adversity, especially early adversity, has a corrosive effect, it is equally true that some people, like the ones mentioned here and thousands of others, have overcome and grown from it.

Childhood Adversity Requires More Than Individual Resilience

ACE research shows how experience becomes embedded in our biology and psyche—how childhood becomes embodied.

Recovery from adversity is not about forgetting or papering over the hurts and wounds. Such recovery often takes place in a residential setting, a safe place where truly dedicated and caring people provide many opportunities for reparenting, developing trust, good communication, education, counselling, and a variety of workshops such as those on forgiveness that can help patients grow into the healthy adults they were meant to be. Individual resilience is not enough. Children need people and institutions that give them opportunities to recover.

Adversity is not a witch’s curse, as in Sleeping Beauty; it is not destiny. It is also not necessarily ennobling. It is not one or the other. The human mind is complex. Someone may be highly successful professionally and a failure at personal relationships. Another may struggle with anxiety or depression yet be remarkably generous and compassionate.

You may ask: Do I carry any scars from my childhood? And if so, how have they affected me?

In many cases, adversity predates birth. I shall address that in my next post.

This is a version of The Globe and Mail post. Nov. 30, 2026.

Abate, B. B., Sendekie, A. K., Merchaw, A., et al. (2025). Adverse childhood experiences are associated with mental health problems later in life: An umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analysis. Neuropsychobiology, 84(1), 48–64

Bullis M., Walker H. M., Sprague J. R. (2001). A promise unfulfilled: Social skills training with at-risk and antisocial children and youth. Exceptionality, 9, 67–90.

Campbell JA, Walker RJ, Egede LE. (2016). Associations between adverse childhood experiences, high-risk behaviors, and morbidity in adulthood. Am J Prev Med. 50(3):344-352

Ellis, B. J., Abrams, L. S., Tottenham, N., & Frankenhuis, W. E. (2022). Hidden talents in harsh environments. Development and Psychopathology, 34(1), 95–113.

Kim, B., & Royle, M. (2025). Annual research review: Mapping the multifaceted approaches and impacts of adverse childhood experiences—An umbrella review of meta-analyses. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 399–416.

#4705. I’ve Hiked All 7 Continents—This Is the Cold-Weather Boot I Recommend for Winter Treks

And more winter hiking gear we pack for every cold trek.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WE’RE HALFWAY THROUGH fall (seriously?!), and that means winter is just around the corner. Colder weather and—depending on where you live and hike—snow, freezing rain, ice, and sleet are all very real possibilities on the trail in the coming months. It’s time to pack away most of your three-season hiking gear and bust out your dedicated cold-weather kit.

Prepping for winter hiking is all about staying dry, warm, and comfortable. Whether you’re looking to upgrade your current outerwear—everything from jackets and hats to hiking boots and socks—or this is your first winter hiking season, we’ve rounded up the best cold-weather hiking gear to help you tackle the trail this year. As a seasoned hiker who’s explored all seven continents over the last 30 years, this is what I recommend in 2026.

Rugged, weatherproof, and ready for the nastiest winter conditions, this new-for-2026 boot is one winter hiking boot to rule them all. But, don’t let the chunky design fool you. These are among the most comfortable, streamlined cold-weather kicks I’ve ever worn (weighing 17.5 ounces), making them versatile enough for not only winter, but challenging shoulder season hikes too.

Like most everything in Paka’s lineup, the Sol Crew leans on a combination of synthetic and natural fibers, giving you the best of both worlds. The Tencel-meets-alpaca construction is breathable, quick-wicking, and extremely odor-resistant. It feels great against the skin as a true base layer, and the dash of Spandex adds just the right amount of stretch. Plus, it’s versatile enough to double as a sun shirt in warmer weather with UPF 30+ sun protection.

If I had to pick just one favorite Mountain Hardwear jacket, the new go-to StretchDown Jacket gets the nod. It’s warm, packable, durable, and the stretch gives it an edge over most other down jackets, with the athletic fit stretching to accommodate beefier layers in deep cold weather. That’s gotten even better with the latest update to the baffling with DoppleWeave, which catches more down and keeps it from migrating much less—making for less cold spots. Plus, it’s available in Light, Medium, and Big “weights,” so you can dial in the exact warmth level that suits your hiking style.

I’ve worn Mammut’s Runbold IV hiking pants on three continents and they’ve never let me down. This winter-ready version is just as wind-resistant and water-repellent, but the addition of a light fleece liner adds even more comfort and a just-right level of warmth. Three zippered pockets add plenty of storage options, and mesh-lined zippered vents keep you from overheating on the trail. Bonus: It’s all made with eco-friendly, bluesign-certified materials.

Keeping your feet dry at all costs is doubly important in winter when unpredictable conditions can deliver freezing rain, ice, snow, or some combination of all three. These socks are phenomenal in wet, cold weather, making them invaluable for winter hiking. They're like wearing a wetsuit bootie on your feet (except with no hinderance in range of motion).

Smartwool’s soft, natural, Merino-centric collection has been a favorite of mine for more than a decade. This OG base layer offers a more relaxed fit (compared to the suctioned-to-the-body vibe of most thermals) and a midweight warmth that’s perfect for layering under hiking pants, ski pants, or just about any cold-weather bottoms. Plus, Smartwool’s is among the softest Merino on the market.

The two-piece design adds a rolltop outer sleeve to a traditional HydraPak water bladder. The result is a setup that’s designed to keep cold water cold in the summer, but with the added benefit of keeping warm water warm for winter hikes. It also helps ensure that your water supply doesn’t straight-up freeze in deep cold conditions.

I’ve been a fan of Icebreaker’s RealFleece blend for years—it’s softer and more luxurious than traditional wool but with all the benefits of natural Merino. This midweight top makes this the perfect in-between top that layers well (on top or underneath) in colder weather. The half-zip design is also great for quickly dumping heat on the go.

The OG Buff is arguably the most versatile piece of apparel in my pack. This winter-ready version upgrades to Polartec fleece that’s warm, buttery soft, and fast-drying. The stretchy construction allows for wearing it any of ten different ways, and UPF 50 protection shields your neck and face on harsh sunny days.

I appreciate a pair of midweight gloves that balances reliable warmth and weather resistance with enough dexterity to allow me to still use my phone, camera, and do the things that heavyweight ski gloves often make impossible on the trail. The Denali checks all of these boxes while adding a silicone grip and touchscreen-friendly fingertips to boot.

Arc’teryx’s Bird Head Toque brings a dash of understated cool to winter hiking headgear, and is amongst the most popular beanies you’ll find right now. I love the oversized classic “dinosaur bird” logo and bold color options. And the blended Merino/acrylic construction ensures that it’s soft, warm, quick-drying, and moisture-wicking—perfect for long winter days on the trail.

Fancy rainshells can be obscenely expensive. Spyder takes most of the next-gen technical features of the best shells I’ve personally tested—four-way stretch, solid DWR, and excellent breathability—and packages them into the surprisingly affordable Clutch that’s available for under $200. Bonus: It ditches the “crinkly plastic bag” vibe of most other rain shells, keeping you quieter on the trail.

Hyperlite leans heavy on next-gen Dyneema Woven Composite 3.9 fabric, ensuring the Southwest 40 is lightweight, extremely durable, and completely weatherproof—all essential for intense winter hikes. I love the roll-top design that keeps things dead simple with just the right amount of organization and nothing more. (I also like that it’s available in 55L and 70L variations for longer expeditions.)

All modern hiking apparel is made from natural fibers, synthetic fibers, or a blend of the two. Merino and alpaca wool are my two favorite natural options, as both offer excellent thermal regulation, breathability, and odor-resistance. They’re fantastic for longer trips, allowing you to pack less and travel farther while staying dry, comfortable, and stink-free. In most cases, however, they tend to be more expensive than their synthetic counterparts.

Synthetic fibers like polyester, nylon, and polypropylene all dry faster than Merino, are typically lighter weight, and more budget-friendly. However, they don’t offer the same odor resistance, and they’re all petroleum-based products. So, they’re hardly eco-friendly.

The key is regulating your body temperature with proper layering. Start with a thin base layer that feels good against the skin and fits closely without being too restrictive. Add an insulating midlayer like a half-zip or full-zip fleece. In especially cold conditions, adding a down shirt or full down jacket will help provide extra warmth. Top it off with a final layer that’s designed for weather protection (to fend off wind and precipitation) in the form of a hard or soft shell. Gore-Tex is the gold standard for this last layer as it offers the best protection, however, it’s also the most expensive. To maintain a comfortable body temperature and ensure you don’t overheat (and sweat), shed or add layers as necessary throughout your cold weather hike. This is where having a little extra room in your pack allows for stashing those extra layers.

There are a lot of individual factors that determine which jacket is right for you, including the quality of down used and how cold or hot you tend to run personally. But fill power is often the most straightforward spec to consider when determining the warmth of a puffy or down jacket. In general, 700 to 800 fill power will keep you warm for most cold-weather hikes. Upgrade to 850-plus fill power for extreme, subzero winter conditions.

It’s also important to consider the face fabric construction. Denier measures both weight and durability. For example, a 7D to 10D down jacket will be lighter and more packable, but also more prone to damage on the trail. Upgrading to a 15D-plus puffer adds weight but also durability. There’s no right answer as it depends on your budget and style of hiking.

Boot insulation is often measured in grams. A winter hiking boot with 200 grams of insulation should suffice in most cold weather conditions, while a 400g+ alternative is better for subzero temps, hiking in snow, or if your feet run cold. A waterproof membrane (again, Gore-Tex is best) is essential for winter boots, especially if you know you’ll be hiking in wet or snowy conditions. Finally, look for an outsole with a winter-centric tread compound with multi-directional lugs (I love Vibram Arctic Grip) for maximum traction in snow and ice.

Whether that’s a weeklong car camping trip or backpacking throughout Utah’s national parks, I’ve assessed outdoor gear in countless different scenarios and climates. #4704. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4703. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4702. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4701. The 91 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 14 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4700. Are You Rehearsing for Your Next Job?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Most people want to advance in their careers. That can mean going from the prep cook to the head chef, from the intern to the CEO (over a very long period), or just getting a slight raise and title bump from where you were two years ago. But whether your aspirations are expansive or just incremental, it's normal to want to feel you are being increasingly valued for what you do. That desire might be practical: Why learn and become a better worker for the same pay and recognition? Or it might be an emotional need to be seen and rewarded. Either way, it makes sense to consider how you can get to your next role.

How we prepare for the next job is not always aligned with what makes us a candidate for the next role from the employer’s side. There are things you can do differently to improve your chances for the next role or promotion. And some of it is more tactical and practical. But some of it requires a different mindset or acquiring skills unrelated to your day-to-day tasks.

See beyond skills. Most of us start with what we know how to do, and try to keep getting better at it. If you're good at sales, you might strive to sell more, or faster, or at higher prices than colleagues. And in the early stages of your career, that's a totally appropriate mindset. In fact, it probably will help you get promoted in the early stages. Do the thing you do better than others, and you will likely see rewards in terms of bonuses and raises, and possibly a promotion. (And if you don’t, that’s a whole other conversation about your long-term relationship with that company.)

The challenge is that by early midcareer, you are likely to need to learn skills like managing people. That's not just the "downstream" people who report to you. That includes managing upstream, which means learning to not only do your job well, but do it in a way that makes your boss's life easier.

Think about it this way: When you're entry-level, your actual contribution is very low. You might not get a ton of credit for things done well. On the other hand, if you make a mistake, it’s probably low stakes. As you get more experienced, your inputs matter. People check your work less. Your contribution is noted, and your mistakes get more costly.

Recognize that promotions require people powers. As you become more senior, you will be expected not only to deliver results, but to know your manager's work style and communication preferences. Adapting to those well can become more critical than just your technical skills.

The ability to deal with people requires a certain amount of emotional strength and good mental health. There’s a reason people complain about “office politics”— and it’s not because it’s rare. Whatever term you want to use, learning to build key relationships with people you might not have a natural connection with is an important (and difficult) skill to learn.

Visualize a role. Another challenge is visualizing the next role in your mind. People understandably get very practical — they focus on a title they want or a certain salary. But they don't picture the whole role. Imagine a job description. It's more than title and compensation. What are the responsibilities? What prior experience is most valuable? Think about what that role entails and what gaps you have now.

A lot of people suffer from imposter syndrome, both in their efforts to be promoted, and even if (especially if!) they actually get the job. Imagine yourself in the role, and practice "acting as if" (yes, it's a real thing to visualize and act as if you are doing the thing you want to do well). It's like rehearsing before a big performance. You won't be less nervous (apparently even Adele gets horrible stage fright – nerves are not about ability), but what it does is let your competence make up for confidence. You can't make yourself "feel" like you're ready for a job. What you can do is practice communication, contributions, and other behaviors necessary for that role. Ideally, by the time the promotion comes, you'll be capable of a lot of the demands, even if you're not yet confident.

Ask yourself why you want the next role. (Hint: money is not enough.) This one can be the toughest because people take for granted that they ought to "want" to advance. Even though it's probably true that many people want to keep getting bigger roles, some people don't. Yes, really — and it's ok if you are one of those people. I once advised a client who had a short list of people they thought would be great to take over the top levels of the company, literally potential C-suite team members, and never thought to ask if they wanted the jobs. I've also worked with someone who knew they didn't want it and was happy to communicate that (they had a parent who had been in the top position, saw what "success" looked like up close, and turned away).

Of course, all of this assumes you’ve stopped and considered if the next role is what you want. Money isn’t nothing — there’s a point at which more money is a real factor and sufficient to keep you motivated. But at some point, many people have enough experience that they could do multiple different things that would earn enough. If all goes well, money stops being the only motivator. So make sure that advancing to the next role is worth it to you in ways that are positive and related to this specific role. For example, believing in the product or service you're working on, enjoying the people you work with, and working with a company whose ethics align with yours are all legitimate and durable motivations. This is what makes the work worthwhile in the long run. Before you commit to the hard work of getting the role, make sure the true payoff is there.

#4699. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.
