#4688. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4687. Who Knew Spirituality Might Prevent Addiction and Relapse?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 13, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I have studied addiction from the laboratory bench to the bedside for more than 50 years. In that time, we’ve learned a great deal about addiction, withdrawal, craving, treatment, and relapse. And we now understand that dopamine, reward, stress, and some brain changes make quitting extremely difficult.

But what is the crux of addiction that makes it so difficult to treat? How do some people stop using while others relapse repeatedly, sometimes fatally?

Alcoholics Anonymous (A.A.) offered an answer long before neuroscientists could look at dopamine in the living brain. Putting a stop to drinking is only the beginning.

When Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith founded Alcoholics Anonymous in 1935, they weren’t thinking about dopamine. They knew addiction and recovery from the patient's perspective. Nearly a century later, neuroscience is catching up. What A.A. called “spirituality” may involve measurable changes in thinking, behavior, social connections, and brain function. A.A. began with clinical observation and lived experience. Modern neuroscience is helping explain why recovery works.

Smith famously summarized A.A.’s core work as simply "love and service." Helping newcomers gives recovering individuals a sense of meaning, boosts self-efficacy (confidence in staying sober), and breaks the cycle of obsessive self-focus.

People might struggle to remember who and what they were before they developed a substance use disorder (SUD). Treatment is tough; it takes time, and people need persistence and resilience. With continued treatment, good things may then happen—relationships, accountability, purpose, and hope.

True, A.A. has spiritual roots, but it’s not a religion. A.A. members are encouraged to find a power greater than themselves. That may be God, or helping others, or something else. Spirituality has always been part of the A.A. founders' core message and approach. Now science is catching up. But what exactly is spirituality doing?

In a recent 2026 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis, Howard Koh and colleagues examined 55 longitudinal studies involving 540,712 people. Religious or spiritual involvement was associated with a 13% lower relative risk of harmful alcohol or other substance use. More-than-weekly religious-service attendance was associated with an 18% lower risk.

Association is not causation, but these are still impressive numbers. People involved in religious communities may also have more supportive families, different friends, greater supervision, and social expectations discouraging drug use, which may influence the numbers.

There’s another important thing to remember about this study. About 87% of the study’s extracted effects concerned prevention. Preventing addiction and treating established addiction aren’t the same thing.

Another study added important information. Paul McClure and Lindsay Wilkinson examined 1,711 adults in the Midlife Development in the United States study. People who attended substance-use recovery groups were 2-3 times more likely to identify as spiritual but not religious. More frequent participation was particularly associated with this identity.

Anyone who has treated SUDs has seen patients who seemed absolutely hopeless. But people surprise themselves and us all the time. They change in ways that cannot be explained by a negative urine drug screen.

Addiction changes priorities. Family, work, relationships, and ordinary pleasures lose their appeal. Behavior and motivation shift from everyday rewards to drugs and drug-related cues.

Drug users remember that drugs produced pleasure. But that becomes a memory. Over time, continued use becomes increasingly prompted by the need to avoid withdrawal, dysphoria, and distress. The next drink, dose, or high takes priority.

Many patients entering treatment are depressed, anxious, and unable to experience pleasure. Some have independent psychiatric disorders. Others have symptoms produced or amplified by chronic substance use and withdrawal.

Detox or cold turkey stopping the drug does not immediately restore normal brain or reward function. This is one reason early recovery is so difficult. The drug is gone, but pleasure, motivation, and hope may not have returned.

We don’t have evidence that prayer restores dopamine neurons or reverses addiction-related neuroadaptations. Those claims would go well beyond the science. But consider what happens in a recovery community. A meeting provides structure. A sponsor provides accountability. A recovering person helps someone newly sober, consolidating their own sobriety. Friendships develop. People resume positive activities they had ended with addiction.

People with SUDs find it hard to believe that helping another person can become more rewarding than getting high. But when they change, helping others can become a reason for living. These changes may be essential to sustained recovery.

The brain learns from experience. Recovery requires new experiences, new habits, and new rewards.

A.A. has been helping people recover since 1935 through personal testimony rather than rigorous clinical research. Then a 2020 Cochrane review of 27 studies found that manualized A.A. and Twelve-Step Facilitation often produced better continuous abstinence outcomes in alcohol use disorder than other established treatments.

John Kelly is the expert on how A.A. works. Kelly says that when social networks change for the better, coping improves. Abstinence becomes more acceptable, and recovery becomes part of a person’s identity. A.A. does not work because someone is told to believe in God (which A.A. does not do). It may work because people change their behavior, their friends, their expectations, and their lives.

Research is finally asking the big questions. Do religious or spiritual involvement reduce the risk of developing harmful substance use? The 2026 meta-analysis suggests it may.

Can A.A. improve recovery after alcohol use disorder has developed? Randomized trials and systematic reviews support that conclusion.

While these are different questions, we know that spirituality is relevant to SUD risk and is also very helpful in SUD treatment.

SUDs develop quickly because of secrecy, stigma, fear, and deep shame. Admitting powerlessness and ceding control to a "Higher Power"—whether defined as God, nature, or the collective wisdom of the group—can help by relieving the crushing burden of trying to control everything alone.

It is up to the individual to figure out. But some patients derive strength from organized religion. Others reject religion but find purpose in service, meditation, nature, family, or secular recovery groups.

What matters most isn’t whether someone attends church. It is whether they have relationships, purpose, and support that help them stay well.

Ask whether religion or spirituality matters to this patient. Has it helped during difficult times? Does the patient want spirituality included in treatment?

Spirituality is not a replacement for medicine, and a sponsor is not a substitute for a physician. Patients with opioid use disorder need medications like buprenorphine or methadone. Severe alcohol withdrawal requires medical detox and naltrexone. Depression, psychosis, and trauma require appropriate assessment and treatment.

Addiction hijacks the brain’s dopamine and pleasure pathways. Spiritual practices like prayer, meditation, and intense fellowship stimulate similar reward and emotional-regulation centers in the brain, affording a healthy psychological substitute. But recovery programs also change how people live, whom they trust, what they value, and what they look forward to.

Stopping drug use is essential, but so is building a life worth staying sober for.

#4686. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4685. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4684. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

They don't make it easy to find out just what that level 3 charging rate is or how big the battery is. If it's as slow as an old Bolt, could take as long as 20 minutes to charge. If the DC charge hardware is more modern, could be 5-10. Would still be a weird choice, but if you need to stop for a drink of a bathroom anyway, why not?

2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV models are expected to begin arriving at dealerships later this year, while the PHEV models are expected to follow in early 2027.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV starts at $32,300 (LE FWD), and the PHEV version starts at $42,100, not including the $1,595 destination fee.

#4683. The Tyranny of Romantic Possibilities

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

James Gibson's influential notion of perceptual affordances refers to the meaningful possibilities for action that the environment offers us. A chair affords sitting, a path affords walking, and a door affords entry. I suggest that this concept can also illuminate the romantic realm. Just as the physical environment presents opportunities for action, the romantic environment presents opportunities for attachment, intimacy, desire, and betrayal. Understanding romantic affordances can help us better understand modern love.

At the heart of Gibson's ecological approach (1979) is the claim that we directly perceive possibilities for action rather than constructing them through complex inferences. Affordances are neither purely objective nor purely subjective; they emerge from the relationship between a person and the environment. Importantly, they do not disappear simply because we fail to notice them. A chair still affords sitting even when no one is sitting on it. Affordances are enduring possibilities waiting to be realized.

This perspective also highlights human freedom. Affordances offer possibilities, not necessities. They present opportunities, while leaving us free to decide which ones to pursue (Ben-Ze'ev, 1981).

"When your heart is on fire, you must realize, smoke gets in your eyes." —The Platters

The romantic environment is rich in affordances. A smile may afford intimacy. A glance may afford hope. An attractive stranger may afford the possibility of a new relationship. While Gibson's affordances involve possibilities for action, romantic affordances also involve possibilities for emotional and relational engagement.

A possibility is not the same as a reality. We are often attracted not to who a person is, but to what they might become in our lives. Sometimes we fall in love with a future rather than with a person. Unlike physical affordances, romantic affordances are notoriously ambiguous. We usually know whether a chair can support our weight. We rarely know whether another person's affection is genuine, fleeting, or merely imagined. Yet this uncertainty is often precisely what makes romantic possibilities so seductive.

Consider the familiar strategy of playing hard to get. By appearing simultaneously available and unavailable, interested and uninterested, people create competing affordances. A related assumption is that "whoever makes the first move loses." In both cases, people hesitate to appear overly eager. Ambiguity heightens desire because the outcome remains uncertain.

People are naturally drawn to what remains unresolved. The incomplete, uncertain, and partly unattainable often generates more emotional intensity than what is secure and stable. Romantic ambivalence thrives on such uncertainty. Robert Greene's (2001) portrait of the master seducer rests on this principle. Mixed signals, delayed gratification, and partial fulfillment keep multiple romantic possibilities alive at once. The attraction often lies less in what has been achieved than in what still seems possible (Ben-Ze'ev, 2024; and here).

"You can't hurry love, oh, you just have to wait. Love don't come easy, it's a game of give and take." —The Supremes

"My lover brings me tranquillity. Not during our lovemaking, which is so exciting, but as an enduring sense of inner peace." —A married woman

Modern life has dramatically expanded the number of romantic affordances surrounding us. Dating apps, social media, and increasing social mobility constantly expose us to potential alternatives. At first glance, this freedom seems desirable. Yet, as Barry Schwartz (2009) argued, an abundance of choice can become a burden. When attractive alternatives are always visible, satisfaction becomes harder to achieve. Instead of appreciating what is good enough, we keep searching for something better.

This abundance also fuels romantic ambivalence. The awareness of alternatives can undermine commitment to existing partners. Research suggests that attraction to attractive alternatives increases uncertainty about one's current relationship and diminishes both personal and relational well-being. The irony is striking: More romantic opportunities may generate greater excitement, but not greater happiness (Zoppolat et al., 2024).

Paradoxically, in a world overflowing with romantic possibilities, calmness and patience become increasingly valuable qualities of profound love (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019). A survey conducted across 116 countries and territories found that 72% of adults preferred a calm life to an exciting one, whereas only 16% preferred the opposite. The appeal of calmness extends far beyond romance.

When possibilities are abundant, the ability to devote oneself to a single relationship becomes especially valuable. Calmness and patience are therefore more than pleasant emotional states. They are ways of resisting the tyranny of endless alternatives. Such calmness is not passive. As Shunryu Suzuki (1970) observed, "Calmness of mind does not mean you should stop your activity. Real calmness should be found in the activity itself."

"True love is not a strong, fiery, impetuous passion. It is, on the contrary, an element calm and deep." —Ellen G. White

Modern romance confronts us with a paradox: freedom can become a burden. The more possibilities we perceive, the harder it may be to appreciate and cultivate the relationship we actually have. Romantic affordances create possibilities. Ambiguity makes them more alluring and their abundance makes commitment more difficult. Mature love requires choosing among them.

Indeed, one of the greatest challenges of contemporary love may not be finding romantic opportunities but resisting them. Never before have so many alternatives been so visible and so accessible. Yet no life, and no love, can flourish by pursuing every possibility. The deepest relationships are built not by maximizing options but by limiting them. A meaningful life and a profound love depend less on keeping doors open than on deciding which door to walk through. In modern romance, the greatest threat may not be the absence of opportunities, but the inability to stop pursuing them.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (1981). J. J. Gibson and the ecological approach to perception. Studies in History and Philosophy of Science, 12, 107–139.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The arc of love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2024). Romantic affordances: The seductive realm of the possible. Philosophical Psychology, 37, 1762-1796.

Gibson, J. J. (1979). The ecological approach to visual perception. Houghton Mifflin.

Greene, R. (2001). The art of seduction. Penguin.

Schwartz, B. (2009). The paradox of choice. HarperCollins.

Suzuki, S. (1970). Zen mind, Beginner’s mind. New York.

Zoppolat, G., et al. (2024). It’s complicated: The good and bad of ambivalence in romantic relationships. Emotion, 24(5), 1190.

#4682. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

Excellent. There are so many warehouses around here, it always baffled me that they weren't all covered with solar panels. Next we gotta get to work on all the parking lots.

Faropoint and SolarKal have not yet announced completion dates, subscription prices, or enrollment details for their New Jersey warehouse roof community solar portfolio.
